title: Stockroom Quorum Read
story: A hardware shop keeps the stock count for each item on 3 replicas. Every write carries a version number one higher than the last, and a write counts as done once 2 replicas have stored it (W = 2). A read asks all 3 and waits for the first 2 answers (R = 2). Because 2 + 2 > 3, the replicas that answer a read always include at least one that stored the latest completed write, so the newest version among the answers is at least that fresh. A replica that is slow or down simply never answers.
This is the quorum read used by leaderless key-value stores (see Replication and Design a Key-Value Store). It only works if the read picks the newest answer, not the first one.
task: Write quorumRead(replies, r). replies lists what each replica sent, in the order the replies arrive. Each entry is [version, value], or null for a replica that timed out.

The coordinator takes the first r entries that are not null, and ignores everything after them, even a newer version, because it has already answered. Return [version, value] for the highest version among those r replies. If fewer than r replicas answered, the read fails: return an empty list.
Two replies with the same version always carry the same value.

examples.explanation: The first reply is version 4 (12 in stock). The second replica timed out, so the coordinator keeps waiting. The third reply is version 5 (9 in stock). That makes 2 replies, and version 5 is newer, so the answer is 9. Returning the first reply, 12, would show stock that was already sold.

The first two replies, versions 7 and 6, already make a quorum of 2, so the coordinator answers with version 7. Version 8 arrives too late to be seen. That is allowed: R + W > N only promises that the read sees the latest write that had finished, and a write still on its way to its second replica has not finished.
Only one replica answered, and the read needs 2. Returning version 3 anyway would drop the overlap guarantee, so the read fails and the caller can retry.

hints: Which replies does the coordinator actually look at? What happens to a reply that arrives after it already has r answers?
Walk the replies in order, skip the nulls, and stop as soon as you have counted r real replies.
While you walk, remember the reply with the highest version so far. Do not sort the whole list: the order of arrival is part of the input.
If the walk ends with fewer than r replies counted, return []. Otherwise return the remembered [version, value].
bruteForce: A tempting shortcut is to return the highest version in the whole list. That is wrong, not slow: the coordinator answers as soon as it has r replies, so replies after that never reach it (the second example).
Another is to return the first reply that is not null. That is a read with R = 1, and with W = 2 on 3 replicas it can miss the latest write entirely (the first example).

walkthrough: Simulate the coordinator: read replies in arrival order, skip timeouts, keep the newest so far, and answer the moment the count reaches r.
• [5, 9]: 5 > 4, so best is version 5. Counted 2 = r: return [5, 9].

Know what this does not give you. R + W > N makes a read see the latest completed write, as long as both quorums are drawn from the same N replicas. It does not order concurrent writes, and a read that overlaps an unfinished write may see it while a later read does not. Real stores narrow that gap with read repair: the coordinator sends the newest value back to the stale replicas it heard from.
solution.timeWhy: One pass over at most n replies, stopping early at the quorum.
solution.spaceWhy: Only the best reply and a counter.
solution.takeaway: With N replicas, W write acknowledgements and R read replies, R + W > N makes every read overlap every completed write, but only if the read returns the highest version it saw, and only once it has heard from R replicas.
